{{Short description|Two closely related series in number theory}}
[[File:Measurement unit.jpg|thumb|A ruler, marked in centimeters (top), and inches (bottom). The rising and falling pattern of vertical lines on the inch scale resembles the ruler function.]]
In [[number theory]], the '''ruler function''' of an integer <math>n</math> can be either of two closely related functions. One of these functions counts the number of times <math>n</math> can be evenly divided by two, which for the numbers 1, 2, 3, ... is
{{bi|0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 4, ... {{OEIS|A007814}}.}}
Alternatively, the ruler function can be defined as the same numbers plus one, which for the numbers 1, 2, 3, ... produces the sequence
{{bi|1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 5, ... {{OEIS|A001511}}.}}
As well as being related by adding one, these two sequences are related in a different way: the second one can be formed from the first one by removing all the zeros, and the first one can be formed from the second one by adding zeros at the start and between every pair of numbers. For either definition of the ruler function, the rising and falling patterns of the values of this function resemble the lengths of marks on [[ruler]]s with traditional units such as [[inch]]es. These functions should be distinguished from [[Thomae's function]], a function on [[real number]]s which behaves similarly to the ruler function when restricted to the [[dyadic rational number]]s.

The 0-based ruler function is also known as the [[p-adic valuation|2-adic valuation]] of its argument,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Erickson |first1=Alejandro |last2=Isgur |first2=Abraham |last3=Jackson |first3=Bradley W. |last4=Ruskey |first4=Frank|author4-link=Frank Ruskey |last5=Tanny |first5=Stephen M. |date=January 2012 |title=Nested recurrence relations with Conolly-like solutions |journal=[[SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics]] |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=206–238 |arxiv=1509.02613 |doi=10.1137/100795425}}</ref> and gives the position of the bit that changes at a given step of the [[Gray code]].<ref name=herter-rote>{{Cite journal |last1=Herter |first1=Felix |last2=Rote |first2=Günter |date=November 2018 |title=Loopless Gray code enumeration and the Tower of Bucharest |journal=[[Theoretical Computer Science (journal)|Theoretical Computer Science]] |volume=748 |pages=40–54 |arxiv=1604.06707 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2017.11.017 }}</ref> The sequence of values of the ruler function is the [[Lexicographic order|lexicographically earliest]] infinite [[square-free word]] over the natural numbers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guay-Paquet |first1=Mathieu |last2=Shallit |first2=Jeffrey|author2-link=Jeffrey Shallit |date=November 2009 |title=Avoiding squares and overlaps over the natural numbers |journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]] |language=en |volume=309 |issue=21 |pages=6245–6254 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2009.06.004 |doi-access=free |arxiv=0901.1397 }}</ref> 

In the [[Tower of Hanoi]] puzzle, with the disks of the puzzle numbered in order by their size, the 1-based ruler function gives the number of the disk to move at each step in an optimal solution to the puzzle.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hinz |first1=Andreas M. |title=The Tower of Hanoi – Myths and Maths | title-link = The Tower of Hanoi – Myths and Maths|last2=Klavžar |first2=Sandi|author2-link=Sandi Klavžar |last3=Milutinović |first3=Uroš |last4=Petr |first4=Ciril |date=2013 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-0348-0236-9 |location=Basel |pages=60–61 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-0237-6}}</ref> A simulation of the puzzle, in conjunction with other methods for generating its optimal sequence of moves, can be used in an algorithm for generating the sequence of values of the ruler function in [[constant time]] per value.<ref name=herter-rote/>
